transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess what brought me in is… I can’t keep my mind on one thing anymore. Like, I’ll be at work trying to fix a rendering bug, and then a Slack ping comes in, or I notice some weird color pattern on the screen, or there’s a siren outside, and suddenly I’m off on some completely different idea before I’ve even finished the line of code. It’s like my attention just gets yanked around.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or hyperactive, like you can't sit still or you're always 'on the go'?

Yeah, definitely. It’s like I wake up with this current already running through me, and my head is full of things I need to do—features I should build, changes in the code, even like… how something could be laid out for an exhibition, or how it would be framed if someone wrote about it. And sitting still just feels wrong, like I’m wasting the moment when there’s all this momentum.
Have you ever had periods where you felt unusually high, extremely energetic, or so confident that you didn't sleep much but still felt rested?

Yeah, I mean… “high” sounds a little loaded, but most days I do feel kind of lit up, like I’m finally moving at the speed everything around me should’ve been moving. Like Glendale finally caught up with what I’ve been building, if that makes sense.

And I do get really confident, maybe too confident, but it feels justified in the moment. Then if my wife or people at work start slowing me down with “process” or meetings or whatever, I snap harder than I mean to. It’s like they’re putting speed bumps in front of something that’s obviously working.
Have you ever had a time when your mood was so high or you felt so powerful that it was noticeably different from your usual self, maybe even to the point where other people commented on it?

Yeah… I mean, people have commented on it. They act like I’m being grandiose or something, but from my side it doesn’t feel random. It feels obvious.

Like, I honestly feel like I’m the only one who can really connect generative art, Mexican visual traditions, and the tech community here in a way that could actually change how the city sees public art. And I know that sounds… big. But I can see the pieces fitting together so clearly, like nobody else is looking at the whole map, they’re all just staring at their little corner of it.
Have there been specific times when your mood was so high, or you felt so powerful or energized, that it was clearly different from how you usually feel day to day—even for just a few days?

Yeah, there have been stretches like that. Most days lately I feel kind of… lit up, like I’m already three steps ahead and everybody else is just now arriving. Like Glendale finally caught up with what I’ve been building, if that makes any sense.

And when I’m in that state, I feel unstoppable. Not just productive—more like it’s obvious what needs to happen and I can see the whole structure of it. But then my wife, or people at work, they start talking about “process” and slowing things down, and I snap harder than I should. It feels like they’re interrupting something that’s finally moving.
Can you think of a time when your mood was so high, or you felt so powerful or energized, that it was clearly different from how you usually feel—even if it only lasted a few days?

Yeah, I mean… yes. It’s not like one single lightning-bolt day, it’s more like these runs where most days I feel lit up, like I’m plugged into something and everyone else is on a delay.

I’ll be walking around Glendale and it feels like the city finally caught up with what I’ve been building in my head, you know? Like all the pieces are right there and I’m the only one moving fast enough to actually do something with them. I feel unstoppable.

But then my wife, or people at work, start talking about “process” and approvals and slowing things down, and I just… I snap. Harder than I mean to. Because in that moment it feels like they’re not being careful, they’re just getting in the way.

Can you recall a specific period — even just a few days long — when your mood was so high, or you felt so powerful or energized, that it was clearly different from your usual self, even for a short time?

Yeah… I know I keep circling it, but yes. There are these periods where most days I feel completely lit up, like I’m moving faster than the room, faster than the whole city almost.

It’s like Glendale finally caught up to the thing I’ve been building in my head, and I’m the one who can actually push it forward. I feel unstoppable in those stretches. Not just confident—more like everything is obvious and waiting for me to act.

And then, you know, my wife will say something about slowing down, or someone at work starts with “process” and approvals, and I just snap. I get way sharper than I mean to, because it feels like they’re blocking the momentum. Like they’re putting cones in front of a train.

Can you think of a specific time when your mood was so high — not just good, but noticeably and intensely elevated — that it lasted for at least four days in a row and was different enough that people around you started acting differently around you, maybe even expressing concern?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, it wasn’t like I woke up one day and said, “This is day one,” you know? It kind of builds, and then suddenly most days I’m just lit up. Like I’m moving faster than everyone around me.

There was a stretch where I felt unstoppable, like Glendale itself had finally caught up with this whole thing I’d been building in my head. I know that sounds dramatic, but that’s how it felt—like all the pieces were lining up and I just needed people to stop dragging their feet.

And that’s when my wife started giving me that look, like she was bracing for me to argue. Same with coworkers—if they brought up “process” or slowing down, I’d snap hard. Not because I wanted to be mean, but because it felt like they were putting up roadblocks right when everything was finally moving.

Can you think of a specific time when your mood was so high — not just good, but unusually and intensely elevated — that it lasted for at least four days in a row and was different enough that people around you started acting differently, maybe even expressing concern?

Yeah… I mean, yes, there have been stretches like that. I’m trying to pin it to one exact block of days, but it kind of blurs because when I’m in it, it doesn’t feel like “a mood,” it feels like I’m finally operating at the right speed.

Most days during those times I feel lit up, like I’ve got this charge running through me, and everything I’ve been building in my head suddenly makes sense. Like Glendale finally caught up with me, if that makes any sense. I know that sounds… big. But it feels true then. I feel unstoppable.

And then people around me start reacting differently, yeah. My wife starts telling me to slow down, or she gets careful with how she talks to me. At work, if coworkers bring up “process” or approvals, I just snap. Harder than I mean to. Because in that moment it doesn’t feel like caution, it feels like they’re standing in the way.

Can you clearly identify a specific stretch of at least four days in a row when your mood was unusually high, and people around you began to act differently because of it — like being concerned or trying to slow you down?

Yes… yes, there was a stretch like that. I’m bad at pinning the calendar to it, because when it’s happening I’m not thinking, “This is day four,” I’m thinking everything is finally moving the way it’s supposed to.

But most days in that stretch I felt lit up, like completely switched on. Unstoppable, honestly. Like Glendale had finally caught up with what I’d been building in my head — which sounds ridiculous when I say it in this chair, but at the time it felt obvious.

And people did act different. My wife kept trying to slow me down, kind of choosing her words carefully, and at work if people started talking about “process” or approvals, I’d snap hard. Like, way harder than the situation probably called for. It felt like they were blocking me, not helping.

Can you think of a specific time when your mood was unusually high — not just good, but noticeably and intensely elevated — that lasted for at least four days in a row, and during which people around you began to act differently because of it?

Yeah, there was definitely a stretch like that. I don’t know if I can give you the clean calendar version, because I wasn’t tracking it that way, but it was more than a few days where most of the day I felt… lit up. Like everything was finally clicking.

It was like Glendale had caught up with this thing I’d been building in my head — which, I know, sounds like I’m making it into some movie or something — but at the time it felt real. I felt unstoppable.

And people did start reacting to me differently. My wife would try to slow me down, kind of carefully, and I’d get really irritated. Same at work. If coworkers started talking about “process” or wanting to slow things down, I’d snap hard. It felt like they were blocking the momentum, not helping.

Can you think of a specific time when your mood was unusually high — not just good, but noticeably and intensely elevated — that lasted for at least four days in a row, and during which people around you began to act differently because of it?

Yeah… I know I’ve kind of said this already, but yes, there was a stretch like that. It wasn’t just being in a good mood. It was more like I was lit up from the inside, like everything was finally lining up and I could see the whole thing clearly.

I kept thinking Glendale had finally caught up with what I’d been building in my head — which sounds strange now, I get that — but at the time it felt obvious. Like I was unstoppable, like if everyone would just stop dragging their feet, it would all work.

And that’s where people started acting different. My wife would try to slow me down, or ask me to pause, and I’d get irritated fast. At work, same thing — if coworkers brought up “process” or wanted approvals or whatever, I’d snap hard. I’d take it like they were blocking me, not helping.

Can you recall a specific time when your mood was unusually high — not just good, but noticeably and intensely elevated — that lasted for at least four days in a row, and during which people around you began to act differently because of it?

Yeah, I mean… yes. I know I’m circling it, but there was a stretch where most days I felt really lit up, not just happy. More like switched on, like I could push through anything.

The way I kept thinking about it was that Glendale had finally caught up with what I’d been building in my head. I know that sounds kind of grand when I say it out loud, but at the time it felt obvious, like everyone else was just moving too slow.

And that’s when people started reacting. My wife would try to slow me down, and at work people would bring up “process” or needing to pause, and I’d snap hard. I didn’t take it as concern then — I took it like they were getting in the way.

Can you recall a specific time when your mood was unusually high — not just good, but noticeably and intensely elevated — that lasted for at least four days in a row, and during which people around you began to act differently because of it?

Yeah, that happened. I know I keep coming back to this, but it’s the clearest example I can think of.

For several days — more than just a good afternoon or something — I felt lit up, like I had this engine in me. I was convinced Glendale had finally caught up with what I’d been building, like the whole thing was right there and everyone else just needed to move with it.

But when my wife tried to slow me down, or people at work started talking about “process” and steps and approvals, I’d snap. Hard. It felt like they were throwing brakes on something important, not like they were trying to help.
After one of these high periods, have you ever experienced a time when your mood dropped significantly—feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

I’m not sure I can pin that down cleanly. Like, after those times, I’d definitely feel… worn out, I guess, or like everyone was looking at me differently, but I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless exactly.

I mean, losing interest in things — maybe? It’s hard because with work, even when I’m not into it, there’s always some ticket or deadline or someone asking for something, so you just keep going. And at home, it’s not like life pauses so you can sit there and measure your mood.

So… I don’t know. I can’t say there was a clear crash like that, not one I’m sure about.
Have you ever had a time when, after one of these high periods, you felt extremely down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for a period of at least two weeks?

I don’t know that I can say “at least two weeks” with any confidence. I mean, after those high stretches there’s definitely a sort of… mess to clean up, emotionally and practically, and I’ll feel low or embarrassed or just tired.

But two weeks of being extremely down or hopeless — I’m not sure. Time gets weird with that stuff. Like with work, one sprint runs into the next, and then there’s something with the house or my wife asking if I’m really listening, and I’m thinking about whether I missed an email from three days ago.

So… I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I haven’t really tracked it that way.

Have you ever had a time when your mood dropped so low after one of these high periods that you felt hopeless, struggled to get through the day, or stopped caring about things you usually care about — even for just a few days?

Maybe for a few days, yeah… but I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless in the way people mean that word.

It’s more like the whole room gets quieter after everything was loud, if that makes sense. I’ll sit at my desk and the code is there, the messages are there, but I’m kind of moving through mud. And then I start thinking about what I said to people, or whether my wife is still upset, or if I made some dumb call at work. Actually, our ticket system makes that worse because everything is timestamped, so you can sort of replay yourself making decisions you thought were brilliant at the time.

But stopped caring? I don’t know. I still care. I just don’t always have the energy to act like I do for a bit. So… yes to feeling low and struggling some days after, but I’m not sure about “hopeless.”

Have you ever had a time when, after one of these high periods, you felt so low that you struggled to get out of bed, lost interest in things you normally care about, or felt like nothing mattered — even for just a few days in a row?

I don’t really know. I mean, getting out of bed — some mornings after those periods, yeah, it feels like I’ve got this… weight on me, but I still usually get up because there’s work, and if I don’t answer Slack then it becomes a whole thing.

The “nothing mattered” part is harder. I don’t think I’ve had it like that, or at least I don’t remember thinking it that clearly. Sometimes I’ll just kind of stare at the screen and not care about the thing I’m supposed to care about, but then I’ll get distracted by some build failing or the coffee machine making that weird noise again — which, actually, I’ve been meaning to fix that because it leaks onto the counter and my wife hates that.

So… a few days of feeling really low and slow, maybe. But I’m not sure I’d say I lost interest in everything or felt like nothing mattered.

Have you ever had a time when, after one of these high periods, you felt so low that you had trouble functioning — like getting out of bed, focusing at work, or caring about things you normally care about — even for just a few days in a row?

I’m not sure I can pin that down cleanly. Trouble functioning… maybe in a loose sense, like I’m slower, I’m not really sharp, I’ll read the same work message three times and still not know what they’re asking.

But I don’t think I’ve had, like, days where I just completely couldn’t get out of bed. I still usually get up because the day sort of drags me into it. The dog needs to go out, or there’s some meeting I forgot was on the calendar — and then I’m annoyed because the calendar reminders pop up at the worst time, and I swear half of them are from recurring meetings nobody needs anymore.

So… yeah, I can have a few days after where I’m kind of low and foggy and not caring as much as I normally would. But whether that counts as “trouble functioning,” I don’t really know.

Have you ever had a time when, after one of these high periods, you felt so low that you lost interest in things you usually care about, had trouble focusing, or felt emotionally numb for several days in a row?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed it as, like, “emotionally numb” exactly. That sounds more definite than how it feels to me.

There are stretches where I’m just… dulled out, I guess? I’ll open an editor and just stare at the same function, and then I realize I’ve been thinking about something totally different, like whether I remembered to order dog food or why the neighbor’s car alarm keeps doing that at 6 in the morning. It’s hard to tell if that’s low mood or just being exhausted after running too hot for a while.

Losing interest… maybe temporarily, but I don’t know. I still care about the things. I just don’t always have the bandwidth to engage with them. Several days in a row? Maybe, but I’d have to think about it. I’m not sure I’ve tracked it that closely.
